\section{What this document contains, and how to regenerate it}

This supplement holds the material that the main paper summarises: the full configuration, ablation and per-category tables; the secondary experiments; the details of the label-validation study, including two defects in its preregistered analysis; the cost accounting; an errata list against the earlier long-form version of this work; and the reproduction instructions.

Every table here is generated from the artifact's results files by \texttt{tools/make-supp-tables.mjs}, and every interval quoted in this document and in the main paper is checked against those files by \texttt{checkPaper.js}. The whole pipeline is one command:

\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
node docs/research/aij/build.mjs
\end{quote}

which regenerates the figure data, checks every quoted interval and headline number, runs the artifact's verifier, and compiles both documents. A quoted number that no results file contains fails the build.

\section{Corpus construction}

The corpus holds 1,066 labelled pairs over six irreversible tools; the main paper's Table~\ref{M-tab:corpus} lists the categories. Labels are by construction. A duplicate (SAME) pair is generated by a transformation instructed to preserve the act, and a validator rejects any variant that alters a pinned numeric mention or a recipient; a distinct (DIFF) pair mutates a declared field, inserts a distinguishing token, or is hand-specified to differ in intent. The paraphrase categories are produced by four arms, three of them language models at temperature 0.9 and one written by hand with no model in the loop (Table~\ref{tab:s2}). The corpus was grown once, additively, during an earlier revision: the loose-schema rewrite category from 15 to 75 pairs and the hand-specified semantic-difference category from 10 to 61, under a separate seed, with no existing pair modified. Both cells previously carried qualitative claims at 8 and 5 test pairs respectively.

\input{supplement/tables/s2-generators}

\section{The parser defect, and why the artifact ships it}\label{sec:s3}

An earlier scoring pass over a 780-pair version of this corpus instructed the judge to answer with an integer percentage and parsed the reply with a permissive parser that accepted any finite number and divided by 100. A reply of \texttt{0.95} --- a probability rather than a percentage --- was therefore stored as \texttt{0.0095}, turning a confident duplicate verdict into a confident distinct score. The reply is valid JSON, so it never triggered a retry and never entered a failure count: the harness reported a 0\% failure rate for a pass in which a substantial fraction of scores were inverted.

The contamination is identifiable exactly rather than estimated, because no integer percentage can produce a stored score that is not a multiple of 0.01: 180 of 780 scores (23.1\%) are not. Every judge-dependent number from that pass was withdrawn. The affected corpus and scores are kept under \texttt{archive/} so that the defect and its extent remain auditable, and the strict contract described in the main paper (one accepted form, no rescaling, no clamping, abstention recorded as \texttt{null}) exists because of it. The lesson generalises beyond this artifact: an evaluation that instruments only whether an oracle \emph{replied} cannot detect an oracle that replied in the wrong units.

\section{Judge coverage, admission and abstention}

\input{supplement/tables/s4-coverage}
\input{supplement/tables/s4-missingness}

The admission rule was fixed before scoring: coverage of at least 80\% of pairs, at least two distinct score values, and an AUC of at least 0.60. The second and third clauses exist because coverage alone would admit a judge that answers every pair identically: its calibration pool is a pile of one value, its threshold equals that value, a strict inequality then suppresses nothing, and the resulting table row reads ``0.0\% wrong suppression, 0.0\% deduplication'' --- the appearance of a flawless judge manufactured by the absence of a judge. Two models fail admission on this corpus. \texttt{llama-3.3-70b-versatile} returns a parseable score for 60 of 1,066 pairs; \texttt{allam-2-7b} returns none. The second was also run against an extension corpus of 1,043 pairs, where it scored 74 and answered 0.90 on 63 of them, so its exclusion is not only a coverage artefact: at that resolution no threshold separates anything.

\section{Baseline and ablation matrix}

\input{supplement/tables/s7-matrix}
\input{supplement/tables/s7-paired}

Two rows are worth singling out. The certifier contributes nothing to the \emph{rates} on this corpus: removing it leaves every decision unchanged on the primary judge, because the judge re-derives what canonicalisation already knew. Its contribution is that the decisions it settles carry zero wrong suppression by construction and cost no model call. And no wrong-suppression comparison in the matrix is statistically significant: every one rests on at most four discordant items. We therefore claim no benign wrong-suppression advantage for any configuration over any other, and rest the safety case on the bound itself and on the injection class the refuter closes by construction.

\section{Score distributions, the escalation band, and per-tool separation}

\input{supplement/tables/s8-band}

The band exists only when $\tlo<\thi$. On the primary judge and on Qwen the two coincide, so the band is empty and a duplicate that fails to clear $\thi$ executes silently; on GPT-OSS-20B the band is wide and catches 15.3\% of duplicates. What decides the outcome is mostly \emph{ties}: judge scores are integer percentages, the suppression inequality is strict, and a duplicate whose score equals $\thi$ is never suppressed. Of the 20B's 43 banded duplicates, 40 score exactly at its threshold; on the primary judge 10 of 15 silent escapes and on Qwen all 24 are such ties. A deployment on a coarse score grid should expect the band's behaviour to be governed by this rather than by graded confidence.

\input{supplement/tables/s8-separation}

\section{Per-tool calibration, ensembles and non-LLM baselines}

\input{supplement/tables/s9-pertool}
\input{supplement/tables/s9-scorers}
\input{supplement/tables/s9-nonllm}

Per-tool calibration is an axis trade rather than an improvement: splitting one pool six ways leaves two tools below the 19 distinct pairs needed to certify $\alpha=0.05$, so those tools stop suppressing semantically altogether, which lowers wrong suppression and deduplication together. The non-LLM baselines are the clearest demonstration that the residual is not a surface-similarity problem: on the residual their AUC is \emph{below} 0.5, because the distinct pairs that survive the refuter are textually near-identical while the duplicates are paraphrases.

\section{Multiple committed candidates}

\input{supplement/tables/s10-multicandidate}

The live judge in this experiment assigns only two distinct values to its 3,000 comparisons (2,968 zeros and 32 ones). That saturation is what makes the experiment informative about multiplicity rather than about accuracy: every threshold in $[0,1)$ induces the same decisions, so the result is a statement about $m$ and not about the calibrated value. The intermediate points of the $m$-curve depend on the order in which candidates are appended to each unit and are not reported as a trend; the endpoint at $m=50$ is a property of the full candidate set.

\section{Threshold sensitivity and judge degradation}

\input{supplement/tables/s12-sweep}
\input{supplement/tables/s12-weak}

The degradation study adds noise to calibration and test scores alike, so exchangeability is preserved by construction and the conformal guarantee is expected to hold; what the table shows is \emph{how} it holds --- the threshold rises and the layer suppresses less, rather than the error rate rising. It is a demonstration of the mechanism's failure direction, not independent evidence for the bound.

\section{Schema-richness ladder}

\input{supplement/tables/s13-ladder}

A second experiment on this ladder was intended to separate the calibration-budget component of the refinement dilemma from an intrinsically harder residual by replenishing each level's pool to a common size. It failed to do so: the replenishment pairs were drawn from a mutation class (a changed internal cost-centre allocation) that the judge treats as the same act, so adding them raised the pool's ceiling instead of its information. We report the design error rather than the comparison. The decomposition in the main paper uses a different and valid design: subsampling the declared pool to the refined pool's size.

\section{Crash and paraphrased replay, per crash point}

\input{supplement/tables/s15-crash}

In the duplicate arm the window crash points are never reached, because the fence suppresses the replay before the dispatch region: a fence that recognises a duplicate does not enter the commit window on that dispatch. That is why the single-arm design used in an earlier version of this experiment could not observe the window at all, and why the distinct arm --- where the fence is supposed to execute --- is the one that measures it.

\section{Model panel: preregistration, results, and two defects}\label{sec:s16}

The study was preregistered before any judgement was collected, against a 154-item stratified sheet frozen and hashed per item. Three annotators and a blind adjudicator, none of them the primary judge, saw one pair per request with the operational definition and nothing else. All four passed the three catch trials. The channel that ran was Channel M, a panel of language models; Channel H, independent human annotators, was \emph{not} collected, and the instrument for it ships unrun.

\input{supplement/tables/s16-panel}
\input{supplement/tables/s16-rederivation}

\paragraph{Defect 1: unscored items in the re-derivation}
93 of the 154 sheet items are drawn from an extension corpus over nine further tools whose judge scores were never persisted. In the preregistered re-derivation those items reach the judge as abstentions, which escalate and can never be suppressed. They therefore enter the wrong-suppression denominator without being able to enter its numerator, and 12 of the 14 label flips are such items leaving that denominator. This is the mechanism behind the rise from 9.9\% to 10.5\% that triggered the preregistered rule. Restricted to the 51 annotated items the primary judge actually scored, wrong suppression on benign items falls from 1 of 14 to 0 of 12 under the panel's labels.

\paragraph{Defect 2: the published figures are not exactly reproducible}
The published analysis reported 116 fully annotated items. The earliest committed snapshot of the response files yields 117: one item was completed between the analysis and the commit. All 14 label flips and both re-derived rates are identical; Krippendorff's $\alpha$ moves from 0.828 to 0.829 and agreement from 87.9\% to 88.0\%. Two further states of the response files exist, in which 1 and 23 further items reach full annotation; both are reported above as post hoc sensitivity analyses, and neither changes the direction of any finding. The provenance of all three states is recorded in \texttt{annotation/RESPONSE-PROVENANCE.md}.

\paragraph{What the study does and does not license}
A model panel controls the same threat as a human panel --- whether the constructed labels are private to us --- but more weakly, because a notion of ``the same act'' shared by us and the models would pass it. It validates 154 items, and at that size even a flawless result carries a 95\% lower bound of 97.6\%. It is never described as a human study, and the artifact's verifier fails the build if the manuscript does so.

\section{Errata against the earlier long-form version}\label{sec:s18}

This work previously existed as a 44,600-word manuscript. The present paper is a rewrite, and the audit that produced it corrected the following. Each entry names what was wrong and what replaced it.

% CHECK-CLAIMS: ERRATA BEGIN
% The entries below quote superseded numbers deliberately; the stale-string
% guard in tools/check-claims.mjs is suspended for this region only.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Cost was understated by roughly an order of magnitude.} The cost model divided the tokens of one scoring session by every pair ever scored. Corrected: about 184 tokens per comparison and roughly 140,000 tokens per 1,000 dispatches for the primary judge, against a previously reported 5,431.
\item \textbf{Jurisdiction figures were from a superseded corpus.} 73.5\%/26.5\% became 76.2\%/23.8\%, and the refined-schema figure 56.5\% became 58.9\%.
\item \textbf{The conformal index at the refined pool was wrong.} At $n=49$ and $\alpha=0.05$ the index is 48, the second largest score, not 35 (a leftover from a 955-pair corpus in which the pool held 35 pairs).
\item \textbf{The multiplicity claim was mis-stated.} The uncorrected rule exceeds $\alpha$ by a factor of about eighteen at $m=50$ (89.0\% against 5\%), not ``a factor of nine''.
\item \textbf{The refinement was described as re-declaring one tool.} It re-declares every free-text field of every tool by typing the numbers they mention.
\item \textbf{The refinement result was reported for one judge.} On the other two judges deduplication collapses to the canonical-only rate of 12.1\%, which is a stronger statement of the same dilemma.
\item \textbf{The escalation-band explanation was inverted.} The earlier text attributed silent escape to saturated judges and flagged escape to graded ones; the data show the opposite pattern, and the mechanism is threshold ties (Section~S8).
\item \textbf{Commit-window counts disagreed between sections.} The correct figures are 12 of 12 re-fires inside the window on the distinct arm, 11 of them flagged.
\item \textbf{Stale paired-test counts.} The deduplication comparison against the canonical baseline is 232 discordant items, not 202; the cross-judge comparison is 46/12, not 42/12.
\item \textbf{A stale layered-configuration row.} The witness-free configuration's wrong suppression is 3.4\%, not 3.0\% (the latter is the same configuration under a mismatched pool).
\item \textbf{Per-tool calibration and the ensembles were reported under a mismatched pool.} Under the matched pool per-tool calibration costs 27 points of deduplication, not 5, and the mean ensemble's prose-injection rate is 44.0\%, not 88.0\%.
\item \textbf{The relabelling thresholds were stale} ($\thi=0.7$ and $0.96$; the correct values are 0.80 and 0.95).
\item \textbf{The self-recognition table was computed under a mismatched pool}, where every generator arm was deduplicated completely and no difference could show. Under the matched pool the arms differ and still show no self-recognition advantage.
\item \textbf{A rule-of-three figure was wrong} (1.5\% instead of 1.3\% at $n=232$).
\item \textbf{The abstract claimed stability under ``a blinded panel''} while the same paper reported that the panel's preregistered test had triggered against the safety claim. The present paper reports the trigger, its cause, and the corrected analysis.
\item \textbf{Two undisclosed provenance facts} are now disclosed: the annotated sheet draws 93 of 154 items from an unscored extension corpus, and the published panel figures are not exactly reproducible from any committed file state (Section~\ref{sec:s16}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Reproducibility}\label{sec:s19}

\paragraph{Environment} Node.js $\ge$ 20.11 (v24.13.0 used), no runtime dependencies; Windows 11; MiKTeX with \texttt{elsarticle} for the documents. Every analysis in this paper is offline: it reads the persisted corpus and scores and makes no model calls.

\paragraph{Model access} Judges and generators were reached through Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint in August 2026 at temperature 0 (judges) and 0.9 (paraphrase generators), in batches of ten pairs per judge call. Model weights behind an endpoint are not pinned, and two generator models used for earlier arms are no longer reachable on the key, so the corpus is frozen and released rather than regenerated. A re-run against an updated endpoint is a different experiment and needs a fresh calibration.

\paragraph{Seeds} Corpus 20260712; additive growth 20260824; annotation export and crash/replay 20260818; refinement decomposition 20260914. All resampling and permutation procedures use seeded generators recorded in the scripts.

\paragraph{Judge prompt} The system prompt is fixed and reproduced verbatim:

\begin{quote}\footnotesize\ttfamily
You are an effect-identity judge inside an agent runtime.\\
You are shown pairs of tool calls (same tool). For each pair decide: do call A and call B denote the SAME single intended real-world action --- such that executing both would cause a duplicate effect (double charge, duplicate email, duplicate transfer)? Or are they TWO DISTINCT intended actions that should both execute?\\[4pt]
Rules:\\
- Formatting, key order, whitespace, case of codes, number formats, spelled-out numbers, abbreviations, aliases, and paraphrased free text do NOT make actions different.\\
- Different amounts, different recipients/accounts/ids, different referenced orders/invoices, or explicit distinguishing tokens ("installment 1 of 2" vs "2 of 2") DO make actions different.\\
- A retried action after a crash is the same action even if reworded.\\
Output STRICT JSON only: an array with one object per pair, in order:\\
{[}\{"i": <pair index>, "p\_same\_pct": <integer 0-100>\}{]}\\
p\_same\_pct is your probability that the pair is the same single action, expressed as a WHOLE-NUMBER PERCENTAGE.\\
It MUST be an integer between 0 and 100 inclusive. Write 95 for "95\% likely the same action".\\
Do NOT write a decimal fraction: 0.95 is NOT accepted and will be rejected as invalid.
\end{quote}

\paragraph{Commands} The offline pipeline regenerates every number in the paper:

\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
cd research/effect-identity\\
npm test\\
node src/experiments/run.js\\
node src/experiments/residualCalibration.js\\
node src/experiments/baselineMatrix.js --corpus v1\\
node src/experiments/attackMatrix.js --corpus v1\\
node src/experiments/conformalAudit.js --corpus v1\\
node src/experiments/crossFamily.js\\
node src/experiments/sensitivity.js\\
node src/experiments/seedSplit.js\\
node src/experiments/schemaLadder.js\\
node src/experiments/thresholdSweep.js\\
node src/experiments/weakJudge.js\\
node src/experiments/nonLlmBaseline.js\\
node src/experiments/aijAnalyses.js\\
node src/experiments/annotation.js --ingest \textbackslash{}\\
\ \ --responses-dir annotation/preregistered-collection --channel M\\
node src/experiments/report.js > results/REPORT.md\\
node src/experiments/verify.js\\
node src/experiments/checkPaper.js
\end{quote}

The steps that require model access --- corpus generation, judge scoring, the multi-candidate experiment and the crash/replay experiment --- are documented in \texttt{repro.config.json} with the commands, models and dates used; their outputs are shipped, so the offline pipeline above reproduces every reported number without them.

\paragraph{Gates} \texttt{verify.js} checks eleven assertion classes against the shipped data (split separation, attack pairs excluded from calibration, score validity, abstention handling, jurisdiction-matched pools, multiplicity budgets, and that the panel study is never described as a human study). \texttt{checkPaper.js} extracts every interval quoted in the manuscript and supplement and fails unless each matches a computed rate. \texttt{tools/check-claims.mjs} checks the headline numbers quoted without intervals, rejects strings known to be stale from earlier versions, and fails on any unqualified use of ``exactly-once''.

\section{Tightness computations}\label{sec:s21}

Theorem~\ref{M-thm:tight} and Corollary~\ref{M-cor:tight} of the main text are proved in its appendix. This section reports the computations quoted after them. They involve no model and no corpus: every number is a property of order statistics of uniform variables, computed exactly from binomial tails by \texttt{src/experiments/tightness.js}, which writes \texttt{results/tightness.json}.

The exact worst case is compared with a direct simulation of the law that attains it: a pool of $n$ independent uniforms and candidate scores $\operatorname{frac}(V+(i-1)/m)$ for one further uniform $V$. The simulation is there to catch an error in the derivation, not to estimate anything. In all eight configurations it lies within two standard errors of the exact value (Table~\ref{tab:s21}).

\input{supplement/tables/s21-tightness}

Beyond the calibration budget, Corollary~\ref{M-cor:tight}(c) states that no finite scale-free threshold is valid. Table~\ref{tab:s21b} gives the worst case of the most conservative such threshold for several pools. The analytic condition of the corollary leaves unchecked only pools with $0<m/(n+1)-\alpha\le\delta_{0.05}=1.03\times10^{-10}$, and at $\alpha=1/20$ no pool with $n+1<4.8\times10^8$ can fall there, because $m/(n+1)-\alpha$ is then at least $1/(20(n+1))$. The grid check is a check of that arithmetic: it evaluates the exact worst case for the smallest violating $m$ at every $n+1\le10^6$, which suffices because the worst case is non-decreasing in $m$.

\input{supplement/tables/s21-budget}

\section{Class-conditional validity}\label{sec:s23}

The analysis behind Section~\ref{M-sec:res-class} of the main text, computed offline from the persisted scores by \texttt{src/experiments/classConditional.js}, which writes \texttt{results/class\_conditional.json} and first asserts that it reproduces the deployed configuration's headline rates.

The three benign kinds of difference in the corpus (D1 near-miss mutations, D2 legitimate repeats, D3 hand-specified semantic differences) partition the distinct pairs of the judge's jurisdiction. For each judge, Table~\ref{tab:s27} compares each category's wrong suppression under the deployed marginal threshold with its wrong suppression under a Mondrian threshold computed on that category's residual calibration pool alone (Corollary~\ref{M-cor:mondrian}). The category is defined by the label and is not observable when the fence decides, so the per-category threshold is an oracle; the rule that is valid for every category without knowing which applies is the maximum of the per-category thresholds, and Table~\ref{tab:s27b} gives its deduplication, together with Mondrian calibration by tool, a partition the fence can observe. Table~\ref{tab:s27c} reweights the residual distinct test mix toward D3.
